hints: Look at molecule A - it is made of two ring sugars joined together, so what is the special name for the bond that joins two monosaccharides by condensation?
walkthrough:
Recognise Two Sugars Joined Together**
Molecule A has a 6-sided ring joined to a 5-sided ring. That is glucose joined to fructose to make sucrose, a disaccharide. When two monosaccharides join, water is removed in a condensation reaction.

Name The Link**
The C-O-C link between two sugars is always called a glycosidic bond. The arrow is pointing exactly to that link between the two rings.

hints: Scan along the long hydrocarbon tail of B and check how the carbons are linked - are any carbons joined by anything other than single bonds?
walkthrough:
What Saturated Means**
Saturated means saturated with hydrogen. Each carbon can make four bonds. If carbons are joined only by single bonds, each carbon still has room for two hydrogens.

Check Molecule B**
In B every C-C link in the long chain is a single bond. There is no C=C double bond, so no hydrogens are missing. That is why it is saturated.
Final answer: no C=C double bonds in the hydrocarbon chain, each carbon has the maximum number of hydrogens

hints: Molecule D is a straight chain of many identical 6-sided sugars linked end to end - think about which glucose isomer makes straight chains for structure rather than coiled chains for storage.
walkthrough:
Spot The Polymer**
D shows four identical ring units joined by O links, continuing at both ends. That is part of a polysaccharide, so the monomer must be a hexose sugar.

Alpha or Beta?**
The regular straight chain with alternating flipped units is cellulose. Cellulose is made only from beta-glucose joined by 1,4-glycosidic bonds. Starch and glycogen would be made from alpha-glucose.

hints: Hydrolysis of a polypeptide breaks it into smaller pieces - look for the molecule that contains N atoms, a C=O link between two amino acid-like units, and the same backbone as a protein.
walkthrough:
What Hydrolysis Gives**
A polypeptide is a chain of amino acids joined by peptide bonds. Adding water in hydrolysis breaks peptide bonds to give shorter peptides, dipeptides or single amino acids.

Find The Peptide**
Molecule C has two amino acid residues joined by a C=O-N-H peptide link, with free amino ($-NH_2$) and carboxyl ($-COOH$) ends. It is a dipeptide, so it is a hydrolysis product. None of the others contain nitrogen in a peptide backbone.

hints: Cell membranes are made of a molecule with a water-loving head and two water-hating tails - look for the molecule with two long fatty acid tails plus a phosphate and choline head.
walkthrough:
Recall Membrane Structure**
The fluid mosaic membrane is mainly a phospholipid bilayer. A phospholipid has glycerol + two fatty acids + phosphate + a small charged head group.

Match To Diagram**
Molecule E has exactly that: glycerol backbone with two fatty acid tails on top, one saturated and one unsaturated with a C=C kink, and a phosphate-choline head on the left. So E is a phospholipid found in eukaryotic cell surface membranes.

hints: Compare the groups on the molecules - count how many O-H and N-H groups A and C have for bonding to water, versus how much of B is just C-H chain.
walkthrough:
Why A and C Dissolve**
Water is polar and dissolves other polar molecules. A is a sugar with many polar OH groups and C is a dipeptide with polar $NH$, $C=O$ and $OH$ groups. These groups form hydrogen bonds with water, so the molecules are hydrophilic and dissolve.

Why B Does Not Dissolve**
B is a long hydrocarbon chain made almost entirely of non-polar C-C and C-H bonds. It cannot form hydrogen bonds with water and is hydrophobic, so water molecules stay bonded to each other and exclude B. Only the single COOH head is polar, which is not enough to make the whole molecule soluble.

Final answer: A and C are polar / hydrophilic and can form hydrogen bonds with water, B is non-polar / hydrophobic and cannot; e.g. A has many OH groups, B has a long hydrocarbon chain with only one OH
